subject: git-github
question: What is Git?
options: A distributed version control system that tracks changes to files over time
A website for hosting code
A programming language
A type of database management system
explanation: Git is version control software, created by Linus Torvalds, that tracks changes to files over time, letting you see history, revert changes, and collaborate with others. GitHub is a separate, hosted platform built around Git.

subject: git-github
question: What is the relationship between Git and GitHub?
options: Git is the version control software itself; GitHub is a company/platform that hosts Git repositories online and adds collaboration features
They are two names for the exact same tool
GitHub is required to use Git at all, even locally
Git is a product made and owned by GitHub
explanation: Git works entirely locally on its own — GitHub (and similar services like GitLab or Bitbucket) is a hosting platform that stores Git repositories remotely and adds features like pull requests, issues, and Actions.

subject: git-github
question: What is a 'repository' (or 'repo')?
options: A project's folder tracked by Git, containing its files and the complete history of changes
A single file containing all of a project's code
A type of programming error
A cloud storage service unrelated to version control
explanation: A repository is the tracked project itself — the working files plus the hidden `.git` folder storing the complete history of every tracked change.

subject: git-github
question: What's the difference between `git init` and `git clone`?
options: `git init` creates a brand new, empty local repository; `git clone` copies an existing remote repository (and its history) to your machine
They are two identical commands with different names
`git init` only works on GitHub; `git clone` only works locally
`git clone` deletes the remote repository after copying it
explanation: `git init` starts tracking a new project from scratch. `git clone <url>` downloads a full copy of an existing repository, including its entire commit history, from a remote location.

subject: git-github
question: What is a 'commit' in Git?
options: A saved snapshot of your project's tracked changes at a specific point in time, with an associated message
A permanent, unchangeable copy of the entire internet
A synonym for deleting a file
A type of GitHub subscription plan
explanation: A commit records a snapshot of your staged changes, along with metadata like the author, timestamp, and a descriptive message — commits form the building blocks of a project's history.

subject: git-github
question: What is the purpose of Git's 'staging area' (accessed via `git add`)?
options: It lets you choose exactly which changes to include in your next commit, rather than committing every modified file automatically
It's a place to permanently delete files
It automatically publishes your changes to the internet
It has no functional purpose and is purely decorative
explanation: The staging area (or 'index') lets you selectively prepare specific changes for the next commit — useful when you've made several unrelated changes but want to commit them separately and logically.

subject: git-github
question: What is the typical basic workflow to save a change in Git?
options: Modify a file, then `git add` it to staging, then `git commit` with a message
Simply saving the file in your text editor automatically creates a Git commit
Deleting the file and recreating it from scratch
Renaming the entire repository folder
explanation: Git doesn't automatically track every save — you explicitly stage changes with `git add`, then create a snapshot with `git commit -m "message"`.

subject: git-github
question: What does `git status` show you?
options: The current state of your working directory: which files are modified, staged, or untracked
The complete history of every commit ever made
Your GitHub account's follower count
The internet connection speed of your machine
explanation: `git status` is one of the most frequently used commands — it gives a snapshot of what's changed, what's staged, and what's untracked at that moment.

subject: git-github
question: What does `git log` show you?
options: The commit history of the repository, including messages, authors, and timestamps
A list of every file currently in the repository
The repository's remote URL only
Real-time error logs from a running application
explanation: `git log` displays the chronological commit history, which is essential for reviewing what changed, when, and by whom.

subject: git-github
question: What is a 'branch' in Git?
options: An independent line of development, letting you work on changes without affecting the main codebase until you're ready to merge
A physical copy of the repository stored on a different computer
A type of file format
A permanent, unchangeable snapshot of the entire project
explanation: Branches let multiple lines of work happen in parallel — you can experiment or build a feature on a branch without disturbing the main/stable codebase until it's ready to be merged in.

subject: git-github
question: What does `git merge` do?
options: Combines the changes from one branch into another
Permanently deletes a branch with no way to recover it
Creates a brand new, completely empty repository
Uploads your entire repository to a cloud backup service
explanation: Merging integrates the commit history and changes of one branch into another, typically bringing a completed feature branch's work back into the main branch.

subject: git-github
question: What causes a 'merge conflict'?
options: Git can't automatically reconcile two competing changes made to the same part of a file across different branches, requiring manual resolution
You've run out of disk space
Your internet connection dropped during a merge
You've used an invalid commit message format
explanation: When the same lines of a file have been changed differently on two branches being merged, Git flags a conflict and asks you to manually decide which changes to keep.

subject: git-github
question: What is a 'remote' in Git?
options: A reference to a version of your repository hosted elsewhere, such as on GitHub
A physical remote control device
A command that deletes your local repository
A synonym for 'branch'
explanation: A remote (commonly named 'origin') points to a repository hosted somewhere else, like GitHub, that your local repository can push to or pull from.

subject: git-github
question: What's the difference between `git push` and `git pull`?
options: `git push` uploads your local commits to a remote repository; `git pull` downloads and integrates changes from the remote into your local repository
They are the exact same command with different names
`git push` deletes the remote repository
`git pull` only works on Mondays
explanation: Push sends your local commits up to the remote (e.g., GitHub). Pull fetches and merges changes from the remote down into your local branch.

subject: git-github
question: What is the purpose of a `.gitignore` file?
options: It tells Git which files or folders to intentionally exclude from tracking, such as secrets, build output, or dependency folders
It permanently deletes all files listed inside it
It's a file for writing project documentation
It has no real function and is purely optional decoration
explanation: `.gitignore` prevents specified files/patterns (like `.env` secrets, `node_modules/`, or build artifacts) from ever being tracked or accidentally committed to the repository.

subject: git-github
question: Why is it critical to never commit files containing passwords, API keys, or tokens to a Git repository?
options: Once committed, sensitive data remains in the project's history even if deleted later, and can be exposed publicly if the repo is or becomes public
Committed secrets are automatically encrypted by Git with no risk
This concern only applies to private repositories, never public ones
Git automatically detects and removes secrets before every commit
explanation: Git preserves full history — deleting a secret in a later commit doesn't remove it from earlier commits, which remain accessible. This is exactly why `.gitignore` and environment variables (not hardcoded secrets) matter so much.

subject: git-github
question: What is the purpose of a README file in a repository?
options: It provides an overview of the project — what it does, how to set it up, and how to use it — usually the first thing visitors see
It's a required file that Git itself needs to function
It automatically runs the project's code
It stores the project's secret configuration values
explanation: A README (typically `README.md`) is the front door to a project — GitHub automatically displays it on the repository's main page, making it essential for helping others understand and use the project.

subject: git-github
question: What does it mean to 'fork' a repository on GitHub?
options: Create your own copy of someone else's repository under your own account, which you can freely modify without affecting the original
Permanently delete the original repository
Merge two unrelated repositories into one automatically
Report the repository to GitHub for review
explanation: Forking is central to open-source collaboration — it gives you your own copy to experiment with or propose changes to, without needing direct write access to the original repository.

subject: git-github
question: What is a 'pull request' (PR) on GitHub?
options: A formal proposal to merge changes from one branch (often a fork) into another, allowing review and discussion before merging
A request to permanently delete a branch
A private message sent to the repository owner
An automatic process with no human review involved
explanation: A pull request is the standard mechanism for proposing changes on GitHub — it shows the differences, allows comments/review, and lets maintainers approve and merge (or request changes) before anything is integrated.

subject: git-github
question: What's the difference between forking a repository and cloning it?
options: Forking creates a new, separate copy on GitHub under your account; cloning downloads a copy (of the original or your fork) to your local machine
They are exactly the same action, just different terminology
Cloning only works for private repositories
Forking deletes your local files
explanation: A common open-source workflow is to fork (create your own GitHub-hosted copy) AND clone (download that fork locally to work on) — the two steps serve different, complementary purposes.

subject: git-github
question: What are GitHub 'Issues' used for?
options: Tracking bugs, feature requests, tasks, and discussions related to a repository
Reporting a user's account for violating GitHub's terms of service
Automatically fixing bugs in your code
Storing a repository's commit history
explanation: Issues are GitHub's built-in tool for tracking project work — bug reports, feature requests, and general to-dos — providing a structured way for contributors to communicate about what needs attention.

subject: git-github
question: Why does writing a clear, descriptive commit message matter?
options: It helps you and collaborators understand what changed and why when reviewing history later, without having to re-read the actual code diff
Commit messages have no effect on anything and are purely optional text
Git automatically generates perfect commit messages, making manual ones unnecessary
Longer commit messages always slow down the repository
explanation: A vague message like 'fix stuff' provides little value months later. A clear message ('Fix null pointer error in login form validation') makes the project history genuinely useful for understanding past decisions.

subject: git-github
question: What does `git diff` show you?
options: The specific line-by-line differences between your current changes and the last commit (or between other specified points)
The total number of files in your repository
A list of all GitHub users who starred your repository
Your repository's total storage size
explanation: `git diff` highlights exactly what's changed — added, removed, or modified lines — helping you review your work before staging or committing.

subject: git-github
question: What's the key difference between `git reset` and `git revert`?
options: `git reset` moves your branch pointer, potentially rewriting history; `git revert` creates a new commit that undoes a previous one without altering existing history
They accomplish identical results with no meaningful difference
`git revert` permanently deletes the entire repository
`git reset` only works on remote repositories, never locally
explanation: `git revert` is generally safer for shared history, since it adds a new 'undo' commit rather than rewriting existing commits — `git reset` can rewrite history, which is riskier once changes have been shared with others.

subject: git-github
question: What does 'HEAD' generally refer to in Git?
options: A pointer to your current position in the repository's history — typically the latest commit on your currently checked-out branch
The name of the repository's owner
A required file that must be manually created for every project
The very first commit ever made in the repository's history
explanation: HEAD tracks 'where you are' in the repository — usually pointing to the tip of your current branch, and it moves as you switch branches or create new commits.

subject: git-github
question: What does switching to a different branch typically do to your working files?
options: Your working files update to reflect the state of that branch, showing its version of the code instead
It deletes all your files permanently with no way to recover them
Nothing happens to your files; only the branch name label changes
It automatically merges every branch into one
explanation: Switching branches (via `git switch` or `git checkout`) updates your working directory's files to match that branch's latest commit — this is how you move between different lines of development.

subject: git-github
question: On a private GitHub repository, why would you add someone as a 'collaborator'?
options: To grant them specific access permissions to view, and potentially push changes to, the repository
Collaborators have no actual effect on repository access
Adding a collaborator automatically makes the repository public
This only applies to organizations, never individual repositories
explanation: Private repositories restrict access by default — adding collaborators (with configurable permission levels) is how you explicitly grant others the ability to view or contribute.

subject: git-github
question: What is GitHub Actions used for?
options: Automating workflows directly in your repository, such as running tests, linting code, or deploying a website when certain events happen
A feature for messaging other GitHub users privately
A tool exclusively for editing README files
A method for permanently backing up your entire GitHub account
explanation: GitHub Actions lets you define automated workflows (in YAML files under `.github/workflows/`) that run in response to events like a push or pull request — commonly used for CI/CD, testing, and deployment.

subject: git-github
question: What is GitHub Pages used for?
options: Hosting a static website directly from a GitHub repository, often for free
A feature for creating video content
A private messaging system between GitHub users
A tool for managing GitHub billing
explanation: GitHub Pages serves static site content (HTML/CSS/JS) directly from a repository, which is exactly the mechanism this Academy's own website is built to use.

subject: git-github
question: What is 'Markdown,' as commonly used in README files and GitHub Issues?
options: A lightweight markup language using plain-text syntax (like # for headings, ** for bold) that renders as formatted text
A programming language for building full applications
A type of image file format
A GitHub-exclusive proprietary format that works nowhere else
explanation: Markdown is a widely-used, simple formatting syntax — GitHub renders `.md` files (like README.md) into nicely formatted text automatically, and it's also used across Issues, Pull Requests, and many other platforms beyond GitHub.

subject: git-github
question: Why does adding a LICENSE file to a public repository matter?
options: It clarifies the legal terms under which others may use, modify, or distribute your code — without one, default copyright law leaves usage rights unclear
GitHub requires every repository to have a LICENSE file or it won't function
A LICENSE file has no legal significance whatsoever
Adding a license automatically makes your code paid/commercial
explanation: Without an explicit license, default copyright applies, technically leaving others without clear permission to reuse your code even if it's publicly visible. A LICENSE file (like MIT, used by this Academy's project) makes usage rights explicit.

subject: git-github
question: What is the purpose of a 'protected branch' setting on GitHub (often applied to `main`)?
options: It enforces rules like requiring pull request reviews or passing status checks before changes can be merged, preventing direct, unreviewed pushes
It makes the branch completely invisible to all repository visitors
It automatically deletes the branch after 30 days
It has no practical effect on how the repository functions
explanation: Branch protection rules help maintain code quality and stability on important branches by requiring review, passing tests, or other conditions before changes can be merged directly.

subject: git-github
question: Why would you clone a repository with Git rather than just downloading it as a ZIP file from GitHub?
options: Cloning preserves the full commit history and lets you pull future updates or contribute changes back; a ZIP is just a snapshot with no ongoing connection
There is no functional difference between the two options
Downloading a ZIP is always technically impossible on GitHub
Cloning is only available to GitHub's paid subscribers
explanation: A ZIP download gives you a static snapshot of the files at that moment. Cloning keeps the connection to the project's full history and lets you stay updated or contribute back — essential for any ongoing collaboration.

subject: git-github
question: What can you do directly from the GitHub mobile app without needing a computer or the command line?
options: Browse repositories, edit files, review and merge pull requests, and manage issues
Nothing at all — the mobile app is read-only with zero editing capability
Only view your profile picture
Run complex Git commands via a built-in terminal exclusively
explanation: The GitHub mobile app supports meaningful editing and collaboration workflows — browsing code, editing files directly, and managing issues/pull requests — which is exactly why this Academy's contribution workflow supports mobile-only participation.

subject: git-github
question: What does 'starring' a repository on GitHub do?
options: Bookmarks it for easy access later and signals appreciation/interest — it's a lightweight way to save and show support for a project
Automatically clones the repository to your account
Grants you write access to the repository
Permanently subscribes you to receive every single code change by email
explanation: Starring is a simple bookmarking/appreciation feature. 'Watching' a repository is the separate feature for actually subscribing to notifications about its activity.
